strengths: The paper addresses an important and realistic failure mode for 3D hand reconstruction: heavy self- and object-occlusion during hand-object interaction. Using object affordance context as a prior is well motivated for this setting.

The proposed framework is conceptually coherent: VLM/LLM-derived affordance descriptions are encoded with CLIP and used to condition a diffusion prior over MANO pose, then applied as a refinement stage for uncertain/occluded joints.

The reported results show a meaningful gain in the high-occlusion subset, reducing PA-MPJPE from 21.3 mm for HaMeR to 16.4 mm. This supports the central intuition that contextual priors are most useful when visual evidence is missing.
The qualitative examples and controllable generation experiment are helpful for illustrating that the model can respond to affordance-related text such as object size while preserving grasp type.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too limited for the strength of the claims. Quantitative evaluation is on only 300 sampled instances from one dataset, with one main table and very few baselines. The average improvement over HaMeR is small, 8.51 to 8.28 mm, and the paper does not report variance, statistical significance, or whether the high-occlusion subset is large enough to support the claimed robustness.

A major concern is reliance on ground-truth grasp taxonomy from HOGraspNet because VLMs cannot classify it reliably. This makes the test-time setting substantially less realistic and weakens the claim that the method uses VLM-generated affordance descriptions. The paper should separate results using fully predicted affordances from results using oracle taxonomy.

The ablation study is insufficient. There is no breakdown of which affordance components matter, no comparison to categorical grasp labels alone, no oracle-vs-predicted caption analysis, no CLIP/text-conditioning ablation beyond an unconditional IHGen-style baseline, and no analysis of the occlusion detector or the number of diffusion refinement steps.

Important implementation details are missing or underspecified, including diffusion architecture specifics, training schedule, data split sizes after subsampling, optimizer and hyperparameters, 2D fitting objective, runtime, prompts, and how hand/object bounding boxes and SAM2 masks are obtained at test time. This limits reproducibility.

The baseline selection is narrow. Since the method is a refinement module initialized from HaMeR, stronger comparisons would include alternative refinement strategies, recent hand-object reconstruction methods, text/interaction prior methods such as G-HOP-style priors where applicable, and simple oracle/contact or grasp-taxonomy priors.

The evaluation focuses on PA-MPJPE, which removes global alignment effects and may not fully reflect hand-object interaction quality. Claims about functional coherence and plausible grasping would be better supported by contact, penetration, object-relative pose, physical plausibility, and per-joint occluded-region metrics.

The controllability evidence is anecdotal, consisting of a small qualitative size-change example. It does not establish that generated poses reliably follow descriptions across grasp classes, object categories, sizes, or intentions.

The manuscript is concise but at times underdeveloped: limitations and failure cases are absent, the societal-impact/reproducibility discussion is minimal, and some writing/formatting issues make parts of the method and experiment section harder to follow.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: 3D hand reconstruction under severe self- and object-occlusion, where contextual hand-object information is genuinely useful.

The proposed direction of conditioning a generative hand-pose prior on affordance-aware descriptions is interesting and well motivated. The use of object attributes, interaction type, intent, and grasp taxonomy is a reasonable way to make contextual signals richer than simple action labels.
The reported high-occlusion result is promising: PA-MPJPE improves from 21.3 mm for HaMeR to 16.4 mm with the proposed refinement on the sampled HOGraspNet evaluation subset.
The qualitative examples suggest that the method can sometimes correct implausible occluded fingers and produce poses that better match the object interaction.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is far too limited for the strength of the claims. The main quantitative evaluation consists of only one table on 300 sampled instances from a single dataset, with no confidence intervals, no statistical analysis, and no discussion of sample selection. The average improvement over HaMeR is only 0.23 mm, which is very small relative to the baseline error.

The description-generation pipeline uses ground-truth grasp taxonomy from HOGraspNet because the VLM cannot reliably infer it. This substantially weakens the claimed test-time affordance reasoning and may inject privileged dataset annotation into the conditioning signal. The paper does not evaluate performance when taxonomy is predicted rather than given.

There are almost no ablations isolating the contribution of each component. The paper does not separately test text conditioning vs. grasp taxonomy labels, VLM-generated attributes vs. ground-truth labels, CLIP text encoding choices, occlusion detection, noise schedule, or the 2D fitting/refinement objective.

The baseline comparison is weak. The only diffusion baseline is an adapted InterHandGen without text, but the adaptation is not sufficiently justified or described, and there are no comparisons to other hand-object reconstruction/refinement methods or simpler priors using taxonomy labels directly.

The method is under-specified. Important details of the diffusion training objective, architecture, sampling/refinement algorithm, 2D reprojection fitting, visible-joint constraints, optimization schedule, training split size, hyperparameters, and implementation choices are missing, making reproducibility poor.

The paper claims controllability, but the evidence is only a two-example qualitative comparison changing small vs. large mug size. This is insufficient to support a broad claim about controllable or semantically faithful pose generation.

The work relies on several large pretrained models and external tools, including QwenVL2.5, Mistral-7B, CLIP, SAM2, and HaMeR, but does not analyze their errors, computational cost, robustness, or failure modes. In particular, errors in VLM captions or masks could directly affect reconstruction.

The writing is generally understandable, but several claims are overstated, especially “extensive experiments” and “substantial improvements” given the narrow evaluation and tiny average gain. The paper needs a more careful limitations discussion and a clearer account of what is actually demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem in 3D hand reconstruction: recovering plausible hand pose under severe self- and object-occlusion. The focus on affordance cues is well motivated for hand-object interaction, where visual evidence alone is often insufficient.

The central idea of conditioning a diffusion prior on affordance-aware textual descriptions is original and relevant to computer vision. It usefully connects VLM-derived interaction semantics, grasp taxonomy, and generative pose priors rather than treating hand reconstruction as purely geometric regression.

The method is conceptually clean: generate structured affordance descriptions, encode them with CLIP, train a conditional diffusion model over MANO pose parameters, and use the learned prior to refine uncertain or occluded joints while preserving visible evidence.

The quantitative results are promising where the method is intended to help most. On HOGraspNet, high-occlusion PA-MPJPE improves substantially from 21.3 mm with HaMeR to 16.4 mm, and it also improves over a diffusion baseline without text conditioning.

The qualitative examples support the claim that the method can produce more functionally coherent grasps, and the controllability example suggests that the diffusion prior responds to meaningful affordance changes such as object size.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is still limited. Evaluation is reported on only 300 sampled instances from one dataset, apparently using one-tenth of HOGraspNet, with no statistical analysis or broader validation across datasets, objects, subjects, or capture conditions.

The method relies on ground-truth grasp taxonomy annotations because current VLMs struggle to infer them. This weakens the practical claim that affordance descriptions are inferred from a VLM at test time, and the paper should more clearly separate oracle affordance inputs from automatically predicted ones.

The average improvement over HaMeR is small, 8.51 to 8.28 mm, and low-occlusion performance is essentially unchanged. The paper’s strongest case is high occlusion, but this should be framed more narrowly rather than as a broad hand reconstruction improvement.

The ablation study is insufficient. It is unclear how much benefit comes from grasp taxonomy versus object category, shape, size, intention, or interaction type; from CLIP text conditioning versus categorical labels; from the occlusion selection mechanism; or from the diffusion refinement schedule.

The baseline set is somewhat thin. The comparison to an adapted InterHandGen without text is useful, but additional refinement and hand-object reconstruction baselines, including stronger recent hand reconstruction models and text/action-conditioned priors, would make the contribution more convincing.

Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or under-specified, including prompts for QwenVL/Mistral, training losses and schedules, diffusion architecture details, 2D fitting objective and optimization, SAM2 mask usage, and hyperparameter sensitivity for the noise level based on occluded joints.

The paper would benefit from more rigorous evaluation of physical plausibility and hand-object consistency, such as penetration/contact metrics or grasp validity, since the claimed advantage is functional coherence rather than only joint error.
